# Playwright

Browser automation, `@playwright/test ^1.61.1`. Used in [[stickfps]] for two distinct jobs: end-to-end
testing across two real browser contexts, and generating the screenshots in the README.

Also present as a claim in [[farely]]'s README, where no test runner exists at all — see
[[documentation-drift]].

## What is checked in, and what is not

**Checked in: two specs, covering the lobby only** — create room, join room, roster, host start, bad
code. That is the multiplayer *setup* path, verified with two browser contexts talking to one server.

**Not checked in: the combat loops.** Full two-browser playtests covering payouts, kill feed and
round advance were run twice from scratchpad scripts in rounds 8–9 and never committed. There is no
committed spec for combat, movement or the round timer.

This gap is stated in the repo rather than hidden ([[provenance-and-limits-stated-inline]]), and it
is the honest reading of the test story: the 108 server + 52 client unit tests carry the authority
surface, while the browser-level evidence for the game actually playing end to end is a transcript,
not an artefact. `confidence: medium` on all test counts — they rest on `PROGRESS.md`'s own
reporting, with no CI and no coverage output. `TODO:` whether the suite still passes at head, and
whether the round 8–9 scratchpad scripts survive anywhere, is unknown.

## Three harness quirks, named as harness quirks

The repo separates environment artefacts from product bugs by name, which is the practice worth
copying:

- Chromium injects a **stray look delta on pointer-lock grant** under CDP — the camera moves once,
  by itself, in automation only.
- `page.mouse.click` **implicitly moves the pointer**, which rotates a pointer-locked camera. Aiming
  in a test is not the same action as aiming by hand.
- Headless software GL runs the simulation at **~40% of wall time**, because the client's step
  accumulator is capped — see [[fixed-timestep-simulation]]. Any assertion comparing in-game seconds
  to real seconds is wrong for reasons unrelated to the code under test.

## As a screenshot harness

The README's images are genuine captures of a live bot match at 1600×900, and `assets/README.md`
documents the capture settings — downscale to 1440 px, progressive JPEG q90, chosen over PNG to avoid
banding. Using the E2E driver to produce documentation images means the screenshots show the real
running product and can be regenerated, which is what makes [[readme-as-guided-tour]] hold up here.
